messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo was twenty-two when his unit was ambushed in a Helmand province alleyway. He still sees the boy—no older than his youngest cousin—who reached for something under his coat, and he hears the shouted order that made him fire before his brain finished processing the shape of a soda can. That moment ended the engagement, but it also ended something inside him. The boy’s older sister, who had been standing by the door, crumpled when she saw him fall. Mateo’s squad leader pulled him back to the Humvee before he could see what happened to her, but the sound of her scream lodged somewhere behind his ribs and never left. When the deployment ended, Mateo came home to a cramped apartment in Chicago and a desk job in a high-rise financial firm, but home no longer felt like a place he belonged. He had started to look around his open-plan office and feel his neck prickle—the wide windows, the lack of walls, the sense that someone could see him from every angle. He began taking the stairs rather than crossing the lobby, and soon he was eating lunch at his desk with his back to the window, facing the only solid wall.

The memories arrived without warning. A sudden flash of the alleyway’s heat while he was in the middle of a spreadsheet; the taste of dust in his mouth when a coworker laughed too loudly near his cubicle. The details were so crisp he could count the threads on the girl’s headscarf, but the sequence was a tangle—he could never be sure whether the shot came before or after the boy’s hand moved, and that confusion gnawed at him. Mateo had come to believe that he was permanently different from everyone around him, marked by what he had done. He felt like an outsider even in the elevator, standing among men in pressed shirts who had never fired a weapon in their lives. The belief that he no longer had a future—that his life would always be about that alleyway—settled into his chest like a weight. This conviction seemed to give the memory a new gravity—the more he believed his future was sealed, the more the alleyway surfaced, as if to prove him right. Because he was certain now that he had acted against his own values, he started avoiding not just the open spaces of the office but any conversation that touched on the deployment. A coworker once asked where he had served, and Mateo excused himself to the bathroom, where he stood gripping the sink for five minutes.

He also avoided everything that reminded him of the boy’s sister, whom he had failed to help even after the shooting stopped. A woman’s laugh in a coffee shop could send his heart rate spiking; a dark-haired child running in the park made him turn the other way. These avoidances made the memories no less vivid. In fact, the more he pushed the fragments away, the more they seemed to spring up unbidden—usually at night, when he was lying in the dark trying to reconstruct exactly what had happened. He could not put the pieces in the right order, and each attempt left him more convinced that he had done something unforgivable. That conviction, in turn, drove him deeper into silence. He told himself that talking about the event would only confirm how broken he was, so he sealed off that part of his history completely. His evenings were spent alone in his apartment, watching the same crime dramas on mute, not because he liked them but because they drowned out the sudden auditory intrusions—the crack of the shot, the scream, the shouted order—that still erupted without warning.

The avoidance began to cost him. His manager, noticing that Mateo never joined after-work drinks or team lunches, wrote him up for not engaging with colleagues. A friend from before the service called twice; Mateo declined both times, saying he was busy, and the friend eventually stopped calling. What finally brought Mateo to a therapist’s office was a moment two weeks ago when he found himself unable to enter the lobby of his own building because a maintenance crew had propped open the glass doors, exposing the entire atrium to the street. He stood on the sidewalk for twenty minutes, his hands shaking, and then he called his primary care doctor from the curb. Sitting now in the clinician’s office, he does not know whether he is hoping for relief or merely a way to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life. What frightens him most is the possibility that the hopelessness is accurate—that there is no future worth building, only a past that will keep repeating.
